standard.title: Group roles and teamwork
standard.description: perform a range of roles in respectful ways to achieve successful outcomes in group or team movement activities
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have applied strategies to work collaboratively when participating in physical activities (AC9HP2M05). They have experience collaborating but have not yet taken on differentiated roles within teams or considered how role performance affects group outcomes.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students perform a range of roles respectfully to achieve successful outcomes in group or team movement activities.

nodes.label: Cooperative skills in movement tasks
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use cooperative skills to complete a movement task, such as a partner balance, passing strategy or team strategy.
nodes.minimum_width: Use cooperative skills (e.g. communication, support, listening) to complete one partner or group movement task.
nodes.typical_width: Apply cooperative skills across varied partner and group movement tasks, identifying which cooperative skills were most important in each context and why.
wider: Compare the cooperative skill demands across different task types (partner balance vs team game vs performance task) and explain how the demands shift.
Observe and analyse how a team in a game or performance successfully uses cooperative skills, then apply one specific observation to their own group work.

response_modes.reason: Cooperative skills (communication, encouragement, turn-taking, supporting others) need to be named, practised and accumulated as a repertoire. Students who only have 'be nice' as a cooperative strategy have limited capacity to adapt to different group contexts.

success_criteria: Demonstrates at least two cooperative skills during a partner or group movement task.
Names the cooperative skills they used.
Identifies how their cooperative behaviour contributed to the group's success.

nodes.label: Maintaining possession — passing and listening
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can work cooperatively with team members to maintain possession in a game by passing to other players and listening to teammates.
nodes.minimum_width: Demonstrate passing and listening to teammates as strategies for maintaining possession in a small-sided game.
nodes.typical_width: Apply possession-maintenance strategies (passing, communication, positioning) across a range of small-sided games, reflecting on which strategies were most effective in different game contexts.
wider: Analyse possession statistics from a game session (who passed to whom, when possession was lost) and use the data to propose a modified strategy.
Explore how possession-maintenance strategies differ across game types (e.g. basketball vs soccer vs touch football) and explain what changes and what stays the same.

response_modes.reason: Passing and communication during game play require simultaneous execution under pressure. Repeated practice in low-pressure, small-sided formats builds automaticity before students can apply these skills reliably in team contexts.

success_criteria: Passes to a teammate to maintain possession in a game.
Communicates with at least one teammate during a movement activity (e.g. calling for the ball, giving direction).
Reflects on how passing and communication helped or hindered possession maintenance.

nodes.label: Modifying activities for inclusion
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can modify physical activities to ensure that everyone is included, such as changing equipment, rules or playing space.
nodes.minimum_width: Propose and implement at least one modification to a physical activity that makes it more inclusive for a specific player or group.
nodes.typical_width: Identify inclusion barriers in a range of physical activities and propose and trial multiple modifications (equipment, rules, playing space) to address them; reflect on the effectiveness of each modification.
wider: Research how disability sport has adapted mainstream game rules and equipment to enable participation, and apply one adaptive principle to a class activity.
Design a fully modified version of a known game that is accessible to players with a specific additional need, trialling and refining the design based on peer feedback.
nodes.hinge_reason: Inclusion through modification is the integrative outcome of this standard — it requires applying cooperative skills (node 1), game understanding (node 2) and perspective-taking simultaneously. Students who cannot modify for inclusion have not yet demonstrated the full capability demand of this standard, and this directly cascades into AC9HP6M09 which requires more complex and independent teamwork with diverse groups.

response_modes.reason: Modification for inclusion requires students to hold multiple perspectives simultaneously (their own experience, another's need, the game's purpose) and make adjustments that serve all. Structured perspective-taking activities (role swap, scenario analysis) support this integrative thinking.

Inclusion barriers look different across movement contexts — game space, equipment type, physical demand, communication style. Wider students who explore modifications across varied activity types develop more nuanced and transferable inclusion thinking.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Inclusion modification is a rich design space — equipment, rules, space, roles, and communication can all be adapted. Wider students who explore modifications across multiple dimensions and activity types build substantially more sophisticated inclusion capability.
success_criteria: Identifies at least one barrier to inclusion in a physical activity for a specific player.
Proposes a specific modification (equipment, rule or space change) to address the barrier.
Trials the modification and reflects on whether it improved inclusion.
